steps.title: A brand arrives
steps.what: A founder lands from a LinkedIn post, a referral or a free-snapshot invitation. One field: their website.
steps.why: The hook is the Triad itself — not a logo or a website package. The first thing a brand buys is clarity about its own drift.

quote.text: AI lets you ship in weeks. It also ships your drift.

steps.hood: Free and self-serve, so it can run at volume. Cost is bounded per brand: each brand is collected at most once per cache window.

steps.title: A few questions, no sign-up
steps.what: The requester names the brand, says whose it is (mine / a competitor / a client), confirms their email in one click and states the brand's stage and promise. Anyone may audit any brand.
steps.why: Public evidence only, so competitor analysis is a legitimate use. There is no account to game: the account is kept internally and revealed only when needed. Ownership is proved later, when a paying brand connects its own data.

quote.text: The Zero Sprint establishes alignment by design, not by validation.

steps.hood: The one-line promise is stored as the first Assumption claim. Every free run — answers and snapshot — becomes Genesis Triad research data, said plainly on the form.
steps.hint: Try A competitor, then click Confirm email & start collecting

states.label: A competitor
states.note: The requester audits a rival: the promise field becomes optional and the side card explains why that is fine.

steps.title: Collect, then freeze
steps.what: If the brand has no current snapshot, the engine gathers public evidence from six sources and freezes it. If it was scanned within the cache window, everyone gets that same snapshot.
steps.why: Every later score reads this exact snapshot. That is what makes the audit repeatable — and what lets a future change be traced to evidence, not to the AI's mood.
steps.hood: Sources: live site, Wayback archive, Google Maps reviews, LinkedIn posts, Google search & AI overview, a scripted walk of public pages. Personal names removed before analysis. Snapshots are cached per brand domain for 30 days (a setting Felix controls); only paying and monitoring clients can force a fresh run.
steps.hint: Watch the sources complete (or try Already scanned), then click See my snapshot

states.label: Already scanned
states.note: Scanned within the cache window: everyone gets the same cached snapshot, no new collection.

steps.title: The free Triad Snapshot
steps.what: Four of the five alignment signals, scored from public evidence, plus the top drifts. Commitment is shown as unknown.
steps.why: Honest by construction: public evidence cannot see repeat purchase or renewal, so the snapshot says so instead of guessing. That gap is exactly what the paid audit fills.

quote.text: When in doubt, the system defaults to the lowest band supported by evidence.

steps.hood: Each evidence item is classified into a signal and a band by a typed decision model; bands roll up by fixed rules. Each finding also carries a direction — promise ahead of proof (drift) or proof ahead of promise (under-told) — so a high score can still flag over-delivery.
steps.hint: Try the other readings, then on Pulling apart click the first finding

states.label: Almost there
states.note: Mostly aligned; one promise slips at weekends.

states.label: Perfectly aligned
states.note: Promise and proof match on every public signal; the full audit confirms it.

states.label: Over-delivering
states.note: Proof ahead of promise: under-told strengths the brand is not claiming.

steps.title: No source, no finding
steps.what: Every finding opens to its receipts: the claim, where and when it was captured, and the evidence that contradicts it.
steps.why: This is what separates an audit from an opinion. A brand can check every line — and so can Felix.

quote.text: Patterns override opinion. Single incidents do not define alignment.

steps.hood: Verdicts carry a calibrated confidence. A finding needs a repeated pattern, not one review. Raw third-party text is kept only while the snapshot is live; the finding itself is kept permanently.
steps.hint: Click How sure can I be of this score?

steps.title: Same evidence, same score
steps.what: The same audit run five times gives the same score — because evidence is frozen, judgements are recorded and scoring follows fixed rules.
steps.why: This answers the problem with chat-based AI audits: a score that wobbles on its own can't power a Deviation Score. Try “Run it again”.

quote.text: Alignment is therefore not negotiated, it is measured.

steps.hood: Each decision is stored against its exact input and model version. A re-run reads the stored decision.
steps.hint: Try Run it again, then Get the full audit (closing this returns to the finding)

steps.title: From snapshot to diagnosis
steps.what: The hidden account reveals itself with the requester's snapshot history, and the brand upgrades to the Alignment Diagnostic at Felix's published fee.
steps.why: The free snapshot creates the need; the paid audit adds what only the brand has and what only Felix can judge.

quote.text: Principal-led consulting. Start with a fixed-fee diagnostic.

steps.hood: Card or UPI payment, GST invoice. Introductory pricing as on the live site. The free snapshot carries over as the before-picture; a login exists only from here on.

steps.title: Inside evidence and intent
steps.what: The brand connects analytics, uploads business metrics, and each leader answers five intent questions. A session with Felix is booked.
steps.why: Inside data completes all five signals. Leaders' answers become the Assumption Score — what they believed before the evidence.

quote.text: How aligned did we believe we were when we began?

steps.hood: Confidential inputs stay in the brand's private workspace and are never used for another client.
steps.hint: Connect a source and add a leader, then try Ready to submit and click Submit for analysis

states.label: Ready to submit
states.note: Data connected, the founder has answered and the sales lead too; operations is still invited. Submit is now open.

states.label: Submitted
states.note: What the brand sees after submitting: the diagnostic is with Felix, the session is booked, and the signed report comes by email. Felix’s console is never shown to the brand.

steps.title: Felix's review queue
steps.what: Felix sees every paid audit waiting for him, with the proposed score and how many low-confidence calls need his judgement.
steps.why: The engine does the legwork; the principal makes the calls. Free snapshots go out automatically; paid audits never do.
steps.hood: Calls below a confidence threshold are routed to Felix first.

steps.title: The principal's call
steps.what: Felix reviews each signal's proposed band with its evidence and confidence. Two are flagged. He moves Emotional from 2 to 1.
steps.why: Overrides are allowed — and recorded with a reason. Over time, Felix's calls also measure how accurate the engine is.

quote.text: Leadership may override alignment signals only by explicitly acknowledging the deviation.

steps.hood: Every override is logged: who, when, from, to, why.
steps.hint: Click band 1 on Emotional, then Approve & sign

steps.title: The signed report
steps.what: The full Alignment Score with pillar views, belief versus evidence, and corrections ranked weakest-signal first — signed by Felix.
steps.why: The report sells the next step on evidence: GTMicro for targeted fixes, GT90 when drift is systemic.
steps.hood: The report names its snapshot and is re-runnable to the same result.

states.label: Report ready
states.note: What the brand sees when Felix signs: every step done, the score and the first fix at a glance, and one button into the signed report.

steps.title: Keep it aligned
steps.what: Regular re-scans track the score against the belief baseline and flag new drift — like a campaign that breaks the corrected promise.
steps.why: The recurring part. Drift never stops, so neither does the value: each cycle shows what improved and what needs fixing next.

quote.text: Alignment, when treated as a discipline rather than a one-time audit, becomes one of the most powerful safeguards.

steps.hood: Each re-scan is a new frozen snapshot; changes come with an evidence diff. Leaders are not re-asked each cycle: their first answers stay the starting line unless the promise changes, a new leader joins, or at the yearly review. A one-question check-in each quarter catches changes.
steps.hint: Pick a cadence and click Start monitoring, then try Three months on

states.label: Just started
states.note: Monitoring is on: the audit score is the first point, the first re-scan is booked, and the four fixes are being watched.

states.label: Three months on
states.note: The gap has narrowed from 6 to 2, and a new campaign claim triggers a drift alert. The brand decides: fix the ad, or re-baseline because the promise really changed.
